artworks.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
artworks.description: Rubens' Prado sketch for the Torre de la Parada shows the flood survivors casting stones that become a new human race — Ovid's Metamorphoses staged as Baroque energy after the waters fall. Pyrrha kneels beside Deucalion among wreckage while earth repopulates behind them; daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, she is the Greek Eve of the second creation.

artworks.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
artworks.description: Castiglione's Denver Art Museum canvas isolates the couple in a rocky waste as they throw their 'mother's bones' — the stones of earth — that rise as men and women. The Genoese painter makes Pyrrha's share of the oracle as visible as her husband's: she, too, must hurl the stones that remake humanity.

artworks.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha
artworks.description: Solis's woodcut for Ovid's Metamorphoses freezes the oracle's command: husband and wife hurl stones over their shoulders while new bodies form from the ground. The print carried Pyrrha's flood into countless Renaissance editions of the poem — the Hellenic survivor who repopulates the world beside Deucalion.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Book 1 makes Pyrrha and Deucalion the survivors who repopulate the world from stones — the Greek flood told as Rome's foundational metamorphosis, with Pyrrha as equal partner in the second creation.

popCulture.title: Pyrrha
popCulture.description: Daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, wife of Deucalion — the Hellenic flood survivor whose name still marks the Deucalionid line through Hellen.
